name: Satyavan
role: Forest prince and husband of Savitri
summary: Satyavan is the gentle forest prince in the Mahabharata whom Savitri chose to marry. His life is given back after Yama's visit, a story retold in festivals, poems and films.
about: Satyavan appears in the Savitri Upakhyana in the Mahabharata, told by the sage Markandeya. According to the epic, he is the son of the blind king Dyumatsena of Shalva, who lost his kingdom to an enemy and lived in the forest with his wife and son. The text says Narada praised Satyavan's virtues, comparing his courage, wisdom and generosity to great figures, but also said he was fated to die a year after his marriage. In the story, he goes to chop wood one day and falls tired, resting his head in Savitri's lap, and Yama comes in person for his soul. Savitri's persuasion restores his life, and his father regains his sight and throne. The name is read as one who has truth, and Sri Aurobindo's poem treats Satyavan as the soul that carries divine truth into the world.
kidSummary: Satyavan is a kind young prince from the Mahabharata who lived in a forest with his parents. His wife Savitri loved him so much that she followed Yama, the god of death, and brought him back to life. His name suggests truth, and he was fond of horses as a child.

story.title: A forest family
story.text: In the Mahabharata, Satyavan's father was a blind king who lost his kingdom to an enemy. They lived simply in the forest, and Satyavan took care of his parents.

story.title: A boy of clay horses
story.text: The text says Satyavan loved horses as a child and made them from clay and drew them. This gave him the nickname Chitrashva, which means painted horse.

story.title: The wedding
story.text: Savitri chose Satyavan to be her husband. After the wedding she joined his family in the forest, and he was happy and kind to her.

story.title: The long day
story.text: The day Narada had named finally came. Satyavan went to cut wood, felt weak, and laid his head in Savitri's lap.

story.title: Back to life
story.text: Yama came to take his soul, but Savitri's brave words changed his mind. Satyavan woke up feeling confused, and she gently reassured him.

teaches: Be gentle and dutiful to your family
Truth is a good name to live up to
Never give up on those you love

facts.text: In the Mahabharata, Satyavan loved horses as a child, making them out of clay and drawing them, which earned him the nickname Chitrashva.
The Mahabharata says Brahmins named him Satyavan, meaning one who has truth, because both his father and his mother always spoke the truth.
In the Mahabharata, Narada answers Ashvapati's questions about Satyavan with comparisons: as radiant as the sun god, as wise as Brihaspati, as brave as Indra and as patient as the earth.
Narada also likens Satyavan's generosity and power to those of Rantideva, the son of Sankriti, and his truthfulness and respect for Brahmins to those of King Shibi Ausinara.

While splitting wood in the forest, Satyavan began to sweat and felt a pain in his head, as if spikes had been driven in, and he asked Savitri if he could lie down because he had no strength left to stand.
When Satyavan woke, he looked at Savitri again and again, the epic says, like a traveller coming home after a long journey.
Waking up, Satyavan wondered why nobody had roused him after such a long sleep, and he asked where the dark man who had dragged him away had gone.
As night fell, Satyavan worried about his parents, urged Savitri to hurry, and swore on truth that he could not go on living if harm had come to his mother or father.
After his father's sight and throne were restored, the priests consecrated the old king, and the epic says Satyavan was anointed crown prince.
Sri Aurobindo read Satyavan as the soul that has descended into ignorance, and Savitri as divine wisdom come to rescue it.

quiz.q: What was Satyavan's childhood nickname, Chitrashva, about?
quiz.why: He made and drew horses as a child.
Dyumatsena was a blind king of Shalva.

quiz.q: Narada said Satyavan was as patient as what?
quiz.why: In the Mahabharata, Narada compares his patience to the earth's.

quiz.q: What was Satyavan doing in the forest when he grew faint?
quiz.why: He was splitting wood when a pain struck his head and he lay down in Savitri's lap.
